Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> NASA initiated the first in a new 12-test series for the RS-25 engine with a successful hot fire on October 17, 2023, at the Stennis Space Center in Mississippi. The full-duration test ran for 550 seconds, which is longer than the 500 seconds required for an actual launch of the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. This test series is for the final certification of a new, updated set of RS-25 engines, manufactured by Aerojet Rocketdyne, an L3Harris Technologies company, which will power future Artemis missions to the Moon, starting with Artemis V. During the test, the engine was fired up to a 111% power level, replicating the thrust needed for an SLS launch. These new engines incorporate advanced manufacturing techniques, such as 3D printing, to make them more affordable to produce. <2> NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission, the first U.S. mission to collect a sample from an asteroid, successfully returned material from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu on September 24, 2023. [3, 4] After a seven-year, four-billion-mile journey, the spacecraft released its sample return capsule, which landed via parachute at the Department of Defense's Utah Test and Training Range. [3, 4, 11] The capsule, containing an estimated 250 grams (8.8 ounces) of pristine rock and dust collected in October 2020, was retrieved by mission teams and transported to a temporary clean room before being moved to NASA's Johnson Space Center for analysis. [5, 13] Scientists will study the sample to learn more about the formation of the solar system and the origin of organic compounds that may have led to life on Earth. [3, 4] Having completed its primary objective, the main spacecraft was renamed OSIRIS-APEX and has been redirected for a new mission to study the asteroid Apophis in 2029. [3, 4, 6] <3> A United Launch Alliance (ULA) Atlas V 551 rocket successfully launched the SILENTBARKER/NROL-107 mission from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, on September 10, 2023, at 8:47 a.m. EDT. This was a joint mission for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the U.S. Space Force (USSF) designed to enhance Space Domain Awareness (SDA). The primary purpose of the SILENTBARKER satellite system is to provide a space-based capability to search for, detect, and track objects in geosynchronous orbit, enabling timely threat warnings for high-value U.S. assets. By augmenting ground-based sensors, the mission aims to provide continuous, all-weather surveillance. This launch marked the final NRO mission to use an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral. <4> NASA's SpaceX Crew-6 mission successfully concluded a 186-day science expedition on the International Space Station (ISS) with a safe splashdown on September 4, 2023. The crew, consisting of NASA astronauts Stephen Bowen and Woody Hoburg, Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, and UAE astronaut Sultan Alneyadi, landed in the SpaceX Dragon Endeavour spacecraft in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Jacksonville, Florida, at approximately 12:17 a.m. EDT. The mission, which began with a launch on March 2, 2023, involved hundreds of scientific experiments and technology demonstrations. Although initially scheduled to return a day earlier, the splashdown was delayed due to unfavorable weather conditions at the recovery sites. <5> Virgin Galactic's 'Galactic 03' mission, its third commercial spaceflight and eighth overall, successfully launched to suborbital space on September 8, 2023. [2] The flight carried three 'Founder' astronauts: Ken Baxter, Timothy Nash, and Adrian Reynard, who were among the first to purchase tickets, with some having bought them as early as 2005. [1, 7] The VSS Unity spacecraft, piloted by Nicola Pecile and Michael Masucci, took off from Spaceport America in New Mexico. [2, 4] This mission was the company's fourth successful spaceflight in four months. [4, 7] <6> A study published on July 14, 2023, provided a time-resolved analysis of molecular measurements from 27 astronauts, including 8 females and 19 males, before, during, and after long-duration spaceflights averaging 165 days. The research, which utilized data from the Lifetime Surveillance for Astronaut Health (LSAH) and Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA), revealed physiological changes associated with spaceflight at both individual and group levels. Key findings include observed impacts on bone resorption, kidney function, and dysregulation of the immune system. The study aimed to better characterize and detect potential adverse health events to maintain astronaut wellness during extended missions. <7> The U.S. Space Force's Space Systems Command announced it has awarded contracts to United Launch Alliance (ULA) and SpaceX for a total of 12 national security missions. [1] The contracts, funded in fiscal year 2023, are split evenly, with each company receiving six launch assignments scheduled to take place in 2025. [1] The payloads include seven satellites for the Space Development Agency's data relay and missile tracking constellations, as well as two spy satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), designated NROL-64 and NROL-83. [1, 2, 3] Additionally, two classified Space Force satellites, USSF-31 and USSF-114, are part of the mission manifest. [1] These launches fall under the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 program. [1] <8> SpaceX's 28th Commercial Resupply Services mission (CRS-28) to the International Space Station (ISS) successfully launched on June 5, 2023, at 15:47 UTC from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A. [1, 2] The mission utilized a Falcon 9 Block 5 rocket carrying a Cargo Dragon 2 spacecraft (C208), which was on its fourth flight. [1, 5, 7] The launch was originally scheduled for June 4 but was postponed due to unfavorable weather in the booster recovery zone. [1] The Dragon spacecraft delivered over 7,200 pounds (approximately 3,304 kg) of cargo, including crew supplies, scientific investigations, and crucial hardware such as the fifth and sixth ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs) designed to augment the station's power. [1, 3, 5] The spacecraft autonomously docked with the Harmony module of the ISS on June 6, 2023. [1, 7] After 23 days attached to the station, the Dragon capsule successfully undocked and returned to Earth, splashing down off the coast of Florida on June 30, 2023, with more than 3,600 pounds of research and equipment. [6, 9]

The initial images, announced on November 2, 2023, revealed Dinkinesh has a smaller satellite. Further analysis of additional images, revealed on November 7, 2023, showed that the satellite, later named Selam, is itself a contact-binary, meaning it is composed of two lobes touching each other, a first-of-its-kind discovery. These assignments represent the fifth and final order year of the Phase 2 contract. The missions were divided between United Launch Alliance (ULA), which received 11, and SpaceX, which was allocated 10. In total, 48 missions were ordered over the five-year Phase 2 contract, an increase from the originally estimated 34. This test series is for the final certification of a new, updated set of RS-25 engines, manufactured by Aerojet Rocketdyne, an L3Harris Technologies company, which will power future Artemis missions to the Moon, starting with Artemis V. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> NASA's SpaceX Crew-8 mission successfully launched to the International Space Station (ISS) on March 3, 2024, at 10:53 p.m. EST, from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This corresponds to 03:53 UTC on March 4, 2024. The crew for this long-duration science expedition consists of three NASA astronauts—Commander Matthew Dominick, Pilot Michael Barratt, and Mission Specialist Jeanette Epps—and one Roscosmos cosmonaut, Mission Specialist Alexander Grebenkin. The mission, which is the eighth operational crewed flight for NASA under the Commercial Crew Program, is expected to last approximately six months. The crew will conduct over 200 scientific experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory as part of ISS Expeditions 70/71/72. The Crew Dragon spacecraft, named Endeavour, docked with the space station on March 5, 2024. <2> On February 22, 2024, Intuitive Machines' Nova-C lunar lander, named Odysseus, successfully soft-landed near the Malapert A crater in the Moon's south pole region. The mission, designated IM-1, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on February 15, 2024, as part of NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. This historic achievement marked the first landing on the Moon by a privately-owned and operated spacecraft and the first American spacecraft to land on the lunar surface since Apollo 17 in 1972. Although the lander tipped upon touchdown and was resting at an angle, it remained operational, and its payloads successfully transmitted data. <3> Varda Space Industries, a commercial in-space manufacturing firm, successfully landed its first orbital factory, the W-1 capsule, at the Utah Test and Training Range on February 21, 2024. The mission's return was significantly delayed due to regulatory hurdles; an initial plan to land the capsule in September 2023 was prevented by a failure to secure re-entry approval from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the U.S. military. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Boeing's Defense, Space, & Security (BDS) division announced it would record a $2 billion loss in its third-quarter 2024 results. [1, 2] The significant losses are attributed to cost overruns on several fixed-price development programs, including the T-7A Red Hawk trainer, KC-46A Pegasus tanker, MQ-25 Stingray drone, and NASA's Commercial Crew Program (Starliner). [1, 2] The T-7A program incurred the largest charge at $900 million, followed by the KC-46A at $700 million. [1, 2] These financial setbacks are exacerbated by an ongoing machinists' union strike and the decision to conclude production of the 767 freighter, the airframe for the KC-46 tanker. [1, 2] The Starliner program, under a fixed-price contract with NASA, has faced continued challenges, [6, 7, 8] The company's overall financial health is also strained, with its commercial airplanes division reporting a $3 billion loss in the same quarter and plans announced to reduce the total workforce by 10%. [1, 2, 5] <2> United Launch Alliance (ULA) successfully launched its second Vulcan rocket certification flight (Cert-2) on October 4, 2024, at 7:25 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex-41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. [1, 2, 4, 5] This mission was the second of two test flights required to certify the Vulcan rocket for national security missions for the U.S. Space Force. [1, 7, 10] While the launch was successful in placing its inert payload into a precise orbit, an anomaly was observed when material appeared to break away from one of the solid rocket boosters during ascent. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The MilSat Symposium 2025 is scheduled to be held in Mountain View, CA, from October 29-30, 2025, as a key event during Silicon Valley Space Week. The symposium is designed to facilitate collaboration between commercial space companies and officials from the Department of Defense. A primary focus of the event will be on the application of artificial intelligence and the development of space defense solutions, featuring discussions and expert speakers on leveraging AI to improve program development and operations in this sector. <2> The Hubble Space Telescope captured its sharpest image to date of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS on July 21, 2025, providing astronomers with the best view yet of the object. At the time of the observation, the comet was 277 million miles from Earth. The detailed images allowed for a more refined estimate of the comet's core size, narrowing the upper limit to 3.5 miles (5.6 kilometers) in diameter, though it could be as small as 1,000 feet (320 meters). This was a significant reduction from earlier estimates of up to several tens of kilometers. News of the observation and the new size estimates was released on August 7, 2025. <3> United Launch Alliance (ULA) successfully launched its Vulcan Centaur rocket for the first national security mission for the U.S. Space Force, designated USSF-106. The launch occurred on August 12, 2025, at 8:56 p.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex-41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. This mission marked the first National Security Space Launch (NSSL) to be conducted on a Vulcan rocket. The rocket deployed its payload, which included the Navigation Technology Satellite-3 (NTS-3) and a classified spacecraft, directly to a geosynchronous orbit. The NTS-3 is an experimental satellite for the Air Force Research Laboratory, designed to test advanced navigation technologies. <4> NASA's Lunar Trailblazer mission, a small satellite designed to map water on the Moon, was officially terminated on July 31, 2025. [1, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11] The spacecraft launched as a rideshare payload aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on February 26, 2025, alongside the Intuitive Machines' IM-2 mission. [1, 2, 3, 6] Initial contact was established shortly after separation, but communication was lost the following day. [1, 2, 4] Limited telemetry indicated the spacecraft's solar arrays were not correctly oriented toward the sun, leading to a depletion of its batteries. [2, 3, 4] After months of unsuccessful recovery attempts by a global network of observatories, NASA formally ended the mission. [2, 3, 8] Ground-based observations showed the orbiter slowly spinning as it drifted into deep space, eventually becoming too distant for its signal to be recovered. [3, 4, 6, 8] NASA announced the mission's conclusion to the public on August 4, 2025. [1, 3, 5, 10] <5> The four members of the SpaceX Crew-11 mission—NASA astronauts Zena Cardman (commander) and Mike Fincke (pilot), JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Kimiya Yui, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Oleg Platonov—arrived at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on August 1, 2025. Their arrival at Launch Complex 39A took place just hours before their scheduled launch to the International Space Station (ISS) aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft on a Falcon 9 rocket. The mission, which successfully lifted off at 11:43 a.m. EDT, is the eleventh operational crew rotation flight under NASA's Commercial Crew Program. The crew is set to spend several months on the ISS conducting scientific research and technology demonstrations. <6> A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched the Starlink 10-29 mission, carrying 28 Starlink V2 Mini satellites to low Earth orbit. [2, 3] The launch occurred from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, on July 29, 2025, at 11:37 p.m. EDT. The mission aims to deliver five NASA-sponsored payloads to the Moon's south pole, specifically the rim of Haworth Crater, to investigate the presence of resources like hydrogen and water ice and to study the radiation and thermal environment. The delivery includes two rovers—the MoonRanger and another from the Canadian Space Agency—and three scientific instruments: a Laser Ablation Ionization Mass Spectrometer (LIMS), a Laser Retroreflector Array (LRA), and Stereo Cameras for Lunar Plume Surface Studies (SCALPSS). As part of the mission, Firefly's Elytra Dark orbital vehicle will first deploy the Blue Ghost lander into lunar orbit before the lander descends to the surface. The lander is expected to operate for over 12 days, while the Elytra vehicle will remain in orbit to provide communications support. <8> The U.S. Space Force (USSF), in collaboration with the Department of the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office (DAF RCO), announced the eighth mission for the X-37B Orbital Test Vehicle, designated OTV-8. [1, 2, 4] The mission is scheduled to launch on August 21, 2025, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. [1, 3] The flight will test a variety of advanced technologies, including a next-generation laser communications system and the highest-performing quantum inertial sensor ever tested in space. [2, 4, 6, 7] <9> NASA's TRACERS (Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites) mission successfully launched on July 23, 2025, from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The University of Iowa-led mission consists of twin satellites designed to study the interaction between the Sun's magnetic field and Earth's, a process known as magnetic reconnection, to better understand space weather. The spacecraft will fly in a unique tandem orbit over the Earth's northern polar cusp, an area where solar wind can directly enter the atmosphere. However, two days after launch, an issue with the power subsystem on one of the satellites, Space Vehicle 1 (SV1), resulted in intermittent communication, and recovery efforts are ongoing. The second satellite, Space Vehicle 2 (SV2), remains healthy and is proceeding with the commissioning phase.
